The hostel wifi went down at seven, and Rafiq's sociology essay was due on the portal at eleven. Normally he would rewrite each paragraph five times and submit at 11:59, shaking.
This time he tried something his senior Vijay had suggested. He set a timer on his phone for three hours. He wrote the essay straight through, fixed the obvious errors, and stopped when the timer rang. It wasn't perfect. The conclusion was a bit thin, and one example could have been sharper.
At ten, he walked to the library, where the wifi still worked, and submitted.
Then he opened his notebook and wrote under the essay title: Next time: stronger conclusion, pick examples earlier.
Walking back through the dark quad, he noticed something odd. He wasn't shaking. He had done a solid job, and he knew exactly what to improve.

qa.a: He set the timer for three hours.

qa.q: How does Rafiq feel walking back through the quad?
qa.a: He feels calm and satisfied, not shaking as usual, because he did a solid job and knows what to improve.

qa.q: Which parts of Rafiq's new approach worked, and why?

qa.q: How might Vijay feel if he heard how the evening went?

Pema's design class had a poster brief due on Friday, and by Wednesday she had made eleven versions, none of them finished. Each time one looked nearly good, she'd see a spacing problem and start over.
On Thursday afternoon, in the college studio in Bengaluru, her classmate Manoj pointed at the clock. "Give it ninety minutes. Whatever is there at five, you print."
She hated the idea. She tried it anyway. She picked version eight, the strongest, and worked only on that. At 4:40, the fonts still weren't perfect, but the layout was clean and the message clear.
At five, she printed it.
In the corner of her sketchbook she wrote: For next poster: fix the font pairing earlier. Try a darker background.
On Friday the teacher called it one of the clearest in the class. Pema still saw the font issue. But now it was a note for next time, not a reason to start over.

qa.q: How many versions had Pema made by Wednesday?
qa.a: She had made eleven versions.

qa.q: How does Pema feel when she still sees the font issue on Friday?
qa.a: She feels calm about it, because it has become a note for next time instead of a reason to panic and start over.

qa.q: What did Manoj's ninety-minute limit help Pema do?
qa.a: It pushed her to choose the strongest version and finish it, turning endless restarts into a solid poster and a list of improvements.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel when the teacher praises Pema's poster?
qa.a: Manoj would likely feel pleased and a bit proud that his push to print at five paid off.

grounding: It shows a student setting a time limit, submitting a solid version and noting improvements, keeping high standards without paralysis.

This month's statement was due Monday. On Saturday she was still re-checking the decimals she had already checked twice, redoing a table so the columns lined up to the millimetre. Her sister's engagement function was that evening. She texted: Start without me, I'll come by eight.

She sat at her desk, thinking of her sister's face when she walked in late. The columns lined up beautifully. It didn't feel worth it.

Lokesh, Class 9, came in on Thursday. At a classmate's birthday party on Saturday, when the girl's mother asked him if he wanted more cake, he said, "No thanks, Aunty, I'm full of your daughter." He meant to say "full, thanks to your daughter's cake." A few people laughed.

Yamini, 25, came back for her second session. Last time she described lying awake replaying a tense conversation with her manager, sometimes for hours.
This week she tried the plan we made. When she noticed the replay starting, she wrote the thought on a notepad by her bed: Manager thinks I'm careless. Then she gave it a slot: fifteen minutes the next evening at seven, at the dining table, to think it through. After writing, she got up and did something absorbing. Twice it was cooking dal from scratch; once it was a walk around the colony.
She said the thoughts came back, but "they had somewhere to go." In the seven o'clock slot, she noticed half of them already felt smaller.
I reminded her that if the thoughts become constant, or turn dark, she should tell me straight away or call the helpline number I gave her. We meet again in two weeks.

Tuesday night
New trick, day five. I'm Reena, and I've been a champion overthinker since school.
This week's loop: the presentation where my slides froze. I'd been replaying it at the office, on the metro, in the shower.
My friend Mehak, who went through something similar, told me what her counsellor taught her. When you notice the loop, write the thought down in one line. Give it a time slot, like fifteen minutes after dinner. Then do something that needs your hands and eyes.
So tonight I wrote: Everyone thinks I'm unprofessional. Then I made rotis, properly, rolling each one round. By the time I finished, the thought had shrunk. At 9:30, in my slot, I looked at the line again. It looked dramatic on paper.
Mehak also said if it ever gets constant or dark, go see someone. I've saved the number, just in case.

qa.a: Reena wrote: "Everyone thinks I'm unprofessional."

qa.a: Reena felt calmer, noticing the thought had shrunk and even looked dramatic on paper.

Caregiver's note, winter holidays — Disha (Kiran's aunt)
Kiran, 9, is staying with us while her mother is away on a work trip. Every night she has lain awake. Last night at eleven she came to my room. "What if the train crashes? What if Mumma doesn't come back? What if I fail the maths test after the holidays?"
I did not argue with each what-if. I sat on her bed and told her that her mother is safe and will phone every evening.
We made a small routine: warm milk at nine, a video call with her mother at nine-fifteen, then I read one chapter aloud and leave the corridor light on. If a what-if comes, she can whisper it to her pillow till morning.
Tonight she fell asleep by ten. I will keep the routine going until her mother returns.

qa.a: The video call is at nine-fifteen.

qa.a: She felt anxious and frightened, her mind full of what-ifs about her mother's safety and the maths test.

qa.q: Why did the aunt's routine help more than arguing with each worry?
qa.a: A calm, predictable routine and reassurance, with the nightly call to her mother, gave Kiran safety, so the worries lost their grip and she slept.

qa.a: She would likely feel grateful and relieved that Kiran is being comforted, and glad the evening calls help.

grounding: It shows, through a caregiver's note, a child lying awake with what-ifs about failing and her mother's safety, and a calm routine and reassurance helping.

Monsoon diary, Thursday
It rained all night. I, Bidisha, couldn't sleep. When the rain gets loud, my brain asks questions.
What if I fail the science test on Monday?
What if Ma's scooter slips on the wet road coming home from the clinic?
What if the tree outside falls on our roof?
Ujjwal dada heard me turning over and came in. He didn't laugh. He said, "Your brain is like a guard who shouts at every shadow. It's trying to help, but most shadows are nothing."
Then he told Ma, and Ma came and sat with me. She said she drives slowly in the rain, and she was home, right here. We'd revise science together on Saturday.
Now every night it's milk, one story, lights out, and Ma checks on me once.
I feel calm enough to write this. Now sleep.

qa.a: He compared it to a guard who shouts at every shadow.

qa.a: Bidisha felt anxious and unable to sleep, the rain filling the dark with what-ifs about the test, Ma's scooter and the tree.

qa.a: Ma sat with Bidisha, gave honest reassurance, planned Saturday revision and set up a calm nightly routine, which made Bidisha feel safe enough to sleep.

It was harvest time in Arohi's village near Nashik, and her mother worked late shifts at the onion storage yard. Her cousin Sabina didi, home from college, was staying with them.
At ten, Arohi was still awake on her mat. "Didi? What if Aai falls from the loading truck? What if I fail the Hindi test? What if the dogs bark all night and I can't sleep and then I fail because I'm tired?"
Sabina didi didn't say "stop worrying." She lay down beside her. "Your head is ringing alarms. It's trying to protect you. But Aai has worked there six harvests, and she's careful. And you know your Hindi lessons."
Then she called Aai on speaker. Aai's voice said, "Home by eleven, baby. Sleep."
Sabina didi hummed the same song she sang every night that week. By the second verse, Arohi's breathing was slow.

The board exams were three weeks away, and Zainab's room in Barmer was covered in sticky notes. Not study notes. Worry notes.
What if the physics paper has the chapters I skipped? What if the power goes during revision? What if I get less than 80 and Abbu is disappointed? What if the centre is far and the bus is late?

Her brother Kunal came in with tea. "Studying?"
"Planning," she said. "Thinking of everything that could go wrong. So I'm ready."
Kunal looked at the wall. "You've written thirty worries and zero equations."
Zainab stared at the notes. It had felt so responsible, thinking of everything. It hadn't felt like avoiding. But the physics guide was still closed.

In her Bogotá apartment, three days before her university entrance exam, Camila had a list on her laptop. It was titled Things That Could Go Wrong, and it had forty-two items.
Oversleeping. A traffic jam on the Séptima. Forgetting her ID. A question on logarithms. Getting a nosebleed in the hall. Her mind jumping to them one after another, faster than she could type.
Her textbook lay open at the same page it had been on since lunch.
Her friend Sami messaged: "How's revision?" She typed: "Preparing for everything." Then she looked at the list, and then at the page, and felt a cold drop in her stomach. She hadn't prepared for anything. She had only imagined.
Sami wrote back: "Want to do 30 min of logarithms together on video? Just that one."
Camila closed the list. "Yes," she typed.

The hostel study hall at eight p.m. was silent except for pages turning. Pankaj sat at the corner desk with his chemistry notes, but his pen hadn't moved in forty minutes.
In his head: the exam could have questions from the part he didn't understand. He could blank out. His handwriting could be too slow. His rank could drop, and his parents had paid for coaching. If his rank dropped, the college would be worse, the job would be worse...
Vandana didi, the evening warden, noticed his blank page on her round. She crouched beside him. "You've been very still."
"I'm thinking about the exam. All the ways it could go wrong."
"And how much chemistry have you done?"
He looked at the page. "None."
"Worry is pretending to be work," she said gently. "Pick one topic. Just one. I'll check back at nine."
Pankaj opened to equilibrium and, slowly, started writing.

qa.a: His pen hadn't moved in forty minutes.

In their flat in Lagos, Chidi's older brother Daniel was in his final engineering year, and his worry filled every room. He checked the stove before bed, then again. He asked Chidi each morning whether the back door was locked. When the power flickered, he unplugged everything.
Chidi, nineteen and in first year, used to tease him. But this term Chidi noticed a change. Walking to lectures, Chidi's hand kept going to the pocket, checking for keys. At night Chidi got up to look at the stove, even after Daniel had checked.
One Sunday, Chidi said it straight out. "Daniel, I think your worry is rubbing off on me. I check things now. I never used to."
Daniel sat down heavily. "I didn't want that."
"I know."
They agreed on a simple plan: one check of the flat at ten, taking turns, written on a card by the door. Daniel also said he'd talk to someone at the student centre about his stress. The card went up that night.

qa.a: They wrote it on a card by the door.
